title: Cross-examination
summary: Learn to ask the one question that makes the other side wobble, then debate whether video games are good for you.

steps.title: Find the wobble
steps.body:
A good question is worth more than a good speech. Cross-examination means asking the other side a question, not to hear their answer, but to make their argument wobble, to show a listener a spot it does not actually cover.

How to listen for the weak spot: while the other side is talking, do not plan your next point yet. Listen for the word 'always', 'never', or 'everyone', those are the words that break the easiest, since one single case that does not fit knocks the whole claim over. Listen for a reason that only explains part of the claim, not all of it. That gap is where your question goes.

Two examples. If someone claims 'screens are always bad for kids', ask: 'is reading a book on a screen the same as watching random videos for hours?' That one question shows their claim was too broad. If someone claims 'rules are there to keep you safe', ask: 'is a rule that only benefits one person, and not the group, still there to keep you safe?' That question tests whether the reason actually covers every case they said it does.

The question of the week is a hard one: is it OK to break a rule to help someone? Think of a real example, maybe sneaking someone extra help on a test, or ignoring a line to let someone go first because they are hurt. Keep it in mind, since asking exactly the right question is what turns a debate around.

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record part of the debate, or record yourself afterward asking the one question that would have made the other side wobble.
